H1.text: In ordinary numbers, two plus three is the same as three plus two. But five minus two is not two minus five. Sometimes order matters.

H2.text: So what about sets? Does the order ever change the answer?

H3.text: Aarav asked this while revising sets after class.

H4.text: Is A union B the same as B union A? And what happens when he mixes union with intersection?

H5.text: Sets follow a short list of laws. Learn them once, and long set expressions become short.

C1.text: First, order. A union B collects everything in A or in B. B union A collects exactly the same elements.

C2.text: So union is commutative. The order of the two sets does not matter. Intersection is commutative too.

C3.text: Now grouping. Take three sets. Join A and B first, then add C. Or join B and C first, then add A.

C4.text: Either way, you collect every element of all three. So union is associative. The brackets can move. Intersection is associative too.

C5.text: But recall episode eight. Difference is not commutative. A minus B and B minus A are different sets.

I1.text: Next, the special sets. The empty set adds nothing, so A union the empty set is A.

I2.text: And A union U is U, because U already holds everything.

I3.text: For intersection, it flips. A intersection the empty set is the empty set. A intersection U is A.

I4.text: And a set with itself. A union A is A, and A intersection A is A. Doing it twice changes nothing. These are called the idempotent laws.

D1.text: Now the big one, where union and intersection mix. The distributive law.

D2.text: It says: A intersection, B union C, equals A intersection B, union A intersection C.

D3.text: Let's test it with shading. Left side first. Shade B union C. Then keep only the part inside A.

D4.text: Now the right side. Shade A intersection B. Then add A intersection C.

D5.text: Both sides shade exactly the same three pieces. The picture works for any A, B and C, so the law always holds.

D6.text: It works the other way round too. A union, B intersection C, equals A union B, intersection A union C.

K1.text: Side by side. In numbers, multiplication spreads over addition. Two times, three plus four, is two times three, plus two times four.

K2.text: But addition does not spread over multiplication. Two plus, three times four, is fourteen. Two plus three, times two plus four, is thirty.

K3.text: Now you try. For sets, does union spread over intersection, the same way intersection spreads over union? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Yes! With sets, both distributive laws are true. That is one way sets are friendlier than numbers.

T1.text: Remember this. For union and intersection, order and brackets never matter, and each one spreads over the other.

M1.text: Last, the laws for complements, named after the mathematician Augustus De Morgan.

M2.text: Step one. The complement of A union B is everything outside both circles.

M3.text: Step two. Outside A is A complement. Outside B is B complement. Outside both is where these two overlap.

M4.text: Step three. So the complement of A union B equals A complement intersection B complement.

M5.text: In the same way, the complement of A intersection B equals A complement union B complement. The complement flips union into intersection.

M6.text: Quick one. Is the complement of A union B the same as A complement union B complement? Pause and think.

M7.text: No! A complement union B complement is the complement of A intersection B. It also covers the parts inside only one circle.

W2.text: U is one to eight. A is one, two, three and four. B is three, four, five and six. Check De Morgan's first law.

W3.text: Step one. A union B is the numbers one up to six.

W4.text: Step two. Its complement in U is seven and eight.

W5.text: Step three. A complement is five, six, seven and eight. B complement is one, two, seven and eight.

W6.text: Step four. The numbers in both of them are seven and eight.

W7.text: Step five. Both sides give seven and eight. De Morgan's law checks out.

X2.text: Many students move brackets freely, even when union and intersection are mixed. They write A union, B intersection C, as A union B, then intersection C.

X3.text: Test it. A is one, B is two, C is three. The left side is one. The right side is the empty set. Brackets move freely only when the operation is the same.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In PUC board exams, as: verify a law, or prove an identity like De Morgan's. And in JEE Main, as: which set statement is not true.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Simplify this set. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Just B.

A2.text: Both brackets contain union B. So use the distributive law in reverse, and take B outside.

A3.text: That leaves A intersection A complement, union B.

A4.text: A intersection A complement is the empty set. And the empty set union B is just B.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Which law says A union B equals B union A?

Y3.text: Two. What is A intersection the empty set?

Y4.text: Three. Write the complement of A intersection B, using De Morgan's law.
